common_name: Queen of Night Tulip (Near-Black Deep Purple Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 8-9 gardens, tulip bulbs generally need to be pre-chilled or treated as annual bulbs, since winters are usually too mild for reliable natural perennializing.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Queen of Night is one of the most famous single late tulip cultivars, prized for its deep, glossy maroon-purple petals so dark they read as nearly black in the garden, especially dramatic when paired with white or pale pastel companions. It blooms late in the tulip season, extending color after earlier cultivars have finished, and is a favorite of flower arrangers for its striking, almost velvety color. In climates with mild winters, tulips generally perform best treated as a fresh fall planting each year rather than a reliable long-term perennial, since they need a sustained period of cold to rebloom well.

common_name: Apeldoorn Tulip (Classic Large Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Apeldoorn is one of the most widely planted Darwin hybrid tulips, known for large flowers on sturdy, tall stems that hold up well to wind and rain.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Apeldoorn is a classic Darwin hybrid tulip, a group bred for extra-large flowers on strong, tall stems, producing bright, clear scarlet-red blooms that have made it one of the most commercially planted tulip cultivars in the world for mass displays and cut flowers. Darwin hybrids like Apeldoorn also tend to perennialize somewhat better than many other tulip types in climates with adequate winter chill, though in mild-winter zone 8-9 gardens they are still usually most reliable treated as a fresh fall planting.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Angelique blooms late in the tulip season with large, ruffled, peony-like double flowers on stems that may need some shelter from wind given the heavy flower heads.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from strong wind, since the large double flower heads can be heavy. Angelique is one of the most romantic and widely loved tulip cultivars, producing soft blush-pink, densely ruffled, peony-like double blooms that look more like a garden rose than a typical tulip, often with subtle deeper pink and cream streaking. It flowers late in the tulip season and is a favorite for both garden display and cut-flower arrangements, prized for its unusually long vase life among tulips. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted bulb display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

common_name: Red Emperor Tulip (Fosteriana Type Very Early Giant Red Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Red Emperor is a Fosteriana-type tulip prized for blooming very early in the tulip season with unusually large flowers on relatively short, sturdy stems.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Red Emperor, also known as Madame Lefeber, is a Fosteriana-type tulip celebrated for opening enormous, brilliant scarlet-red flowers very early in spring, well ahead of most other tulip types, giving an early burst of bold color while many other bulbs are just emerging. Its wide, bowl-shaped blooms open fully in sun to reveal a black-based interior that adds drama to the display, and the sturdy, relatively short stems hold up well to wind and rain. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed is slow to germinate and seedlings grow slowly at first; transplant out after danger of hard frost has passed, keeping soil consistently moist through the season.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of transplanting, since celery germinates slowly and seedlings need a long head start before warm weather arrives. Tango is a modern celery cultivar bred for compact size, crisp, stringless stalks, and good resistance to common celery diseases that plague older cultivars in humid climates, producing dark green, flavorful stalks over a somewhat shorter growing season than heirloom types. Consistent, even soil moisture is essential throughout the growing season, since celery stalks turn stringy and bitter under moisture stress. In hot-summer regions it does best as a fall or early spring crop rather than attempting to carry it through peak summer heat, since celery bolts and becomes bitter in prolonged high temperatures.
